Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "our neighborhood weather station sits behind the small brick library on Alder Street, in a fenced strip between the community garden and the library's delivery entrance. The station started operating in 2018, after residents raised money for a rain gauge and a school science club offered to help with readings. It is not an official forecasting office, and its figures do not replace the warnings from the regional weather service. Instead, it keeps a local record that people can compare with the broader reports. The library lets the group use its outdoor power outlet, but the equipment shed and the station itself belong to the neighborhood association.

The first setup was a wooden post with a manual rain gauge and a thermometer fixed to it in a way that made reading the thermometer harder than it needed to be. In 2021, volunteers replaced the post and added a digital temperature-and-humidity sensor, a wind vane, and a small solar panel. The panel charges a battery in the equipment shed, and the sensor sends readings to a tablet kept at the library's front desk. The rain gauge is still read by hand, because the group wanted a simple backup record if the sensor or tablet stops working. I usually think this mix is a sensible one, though the tablet can be slow to reconnect after a power interruption.

Mara Chen coordinates the volunteers and checks the station on Tuesday mornings. She said, “The point is to notice what our own block is doing, not to compete with the airport.” That distinction comes up often when neighbors ask why the station's wind reading differs from the number in a regional forecast. The library wall and the garden fence partly shelter the instruments, and the station is lower than the airport equipment. The group records those surroundings on its information sheet so anyone using the figures can understand what they do and do not show.

The weekly routine is shared by six residents and two members of the science club. One person checks the rain gauge, another compares the sensor's time with the tablet, and a third looks for leaves or spiderwebs around the wind vane. They write the date, the time, and any problem in a paper logbook before entering the measurements into a shared spreadsheet. A student usually takes a photograph of the gauge before it is emptied. The photographs are useful when an entry looks unusual, although they do not give a more accurate measurement by themselves.

1. What the station records

The digital sensor reports air temperature and relative humidity every fifteen minutes. The wind vane provides direction, while a separate cup anemometer records wind speed. Rainfall is recorded once each morning, so a shower between checks appears as part of the total for that measuring period rather than as a precise start and stop time. The group stores the original readings and a monthly copy on a library computer. If the tablet is offline, the measurements remain in the sensor's memory, but a volunteer has to reconnect it before they appear in the spreadsheet. The group does not estimate missing readings; it leaves the gap visible and notes why it happened when that is known.

2. Maintenance and access

The neighborhood association pays for batteries, replacement cups for the anemometer, and printing the information sheet. The science club supplies no money, but its teacher lends a handheld thermometer for occasional comparisons. In March, the group cleans the rain gauge and checks that it stands level. A cracked plastic funnel was replaced last spring after water collected unevenly along one edge. The shed key is held by Mara and by the library manager, so a volunteer does not need to enter the library during evening checks. The gate is usually unlocked on weekdays, but if it is locked, volunteers wait for the library manager rather than climbing over it. This matters because the association's insurance does not cover people entering the fenced strip without permission.

3. How neighbors use the information

The library posts a monthly sheet near its noticeboard, with the highest and lowest temperatures, total rainfall, and a short note about missing data. The community garden team consults the rainfall total before deciding whether to water its new beds, but it also checks the soil directly. Last July, for example, the station recorded three dry weeks, while a shaded section of the garden remained damp. Garden coordinator Luis Ortega said, “The sheet gives us a useful nudge, not an instruction.” A teacher at Alder Street School sometimes uses the wind direction readings for a class exercise about maps and observation. The figures are not presented as evidence that one street is warmer than another, since the station has only one location and its setting affects what it measures.

The group has discussed moving the station farther from the library wall, but there is not yet an agreed site with both safe access and permission to install equipment. A spot beside the playing field might give the wind vane more open space, though it would also put the instruments closer to balls and evening events. For now, volunteers have agreed to keep the current setup and add a note to the information sheet about the nearby wall and fence. Mara says she would perhaps revisit the question after the association renews its grounds agreement next year.
